title: How to Be Freer Than a King
author: Daily Stoic
summary: This piece contrasts Epictetus, who spent his first thirty years enslaved yet mastered his own judgments and desires, with the emperor Nero, who commanded an empire yet was ruled by his own appetites, anger, and fear. Drawing on Epictetus's central question, 'Who is your master?', the piece argues that real freedom has nothing to do with external power or possessions and everything to do with self-governance: a person who cannot resist a craving, control their temper, or stop needing others' approval is not free no matter their rank. It quotes Edmund Burke's observation that 'men of intemperate minds cannot be free' because 'their passions forge their fetters,' and lands on Epictetus's core teaching that since we cannot choose our external circumstances, freedom lies entirely in choosing our response to them.
points: The central paradox driving the piece: Epictetus was enslaved for his first thirty years yet free, while Nero commanded an empire yet was 'ruled by his appetites, his anger, his vanity, and his fear.'
Edmund Burke's line is used to generalize the Stoic claim beyond antiquity: 'Men of intemperate minds cannot be free. Their passions forge their fetters.'

The piece operationalizes freedom into concrete behavioral tests: 'the person who must concede to every craving is not free. The person who explodes whenever they are angry is not free. The person who needs applause, attention, or approval is not free.'
Epictetus's core teaching is distilled into a locus-of-control principle: since 'we cannot choose our external circumstances,' freedom consists entirely in 'how we respond to them.'
quotes: Nero could command armies, order executions, and bend an empire to his will. But he could not govern himself.
Men of intemperate minds cannot be free. Their passions forge their fetters.
We often imagine that freedom means having more power, more money, or fewer people telling us what to do.
You can rule an empire and still live in chains. You can own almost nothing and still be freer than a king.
Freedom, for the Stoics, is mastering yourself and how you respond to fate.
We cannot choose our external circumstances, he said, we can always choose how we respond to them. And there is freedom in that.
